questions.question: Which of the following best describes a consequence of separating the control and data planes in SDN?
options: It enforces uniform packet size across all switches
It eliminates the need for routing protocols entirely
It requires every packet to be processed by a central controller
It restricts the use of standard Ethernet in the data plane
It enables centralized control while keeping forwarding distributed
questions.explanation:
SDN separates the logic choosing forwarding behavior from the devices that apply it to individual packets. A logically centralized control plane can therefore program several switches while those switches continue distributed packet forwarding. Logical centralization does not require one physical controller machine, and normal matching traffic need not visit the controller for every packet.

See [SDN separation, logical centralization, and interfaces](../lessons/06_sdn/01_definition_and_interfaces.md).

questions.question: How does SDN architecture differ structurally from traditional networking architectures?
options: SDN prohibits software-based routers in enterprise networks
SDN uses static routing tables hardcoded into ASICs
SDN duplicates forwarding logic across all routers
SDN delegates control decisions to forwarding hardware
SDN consolidates control logic into a logically centralized controller
questions.explanation:
The architecture moves control decisions out of independent per-device control processes into a logically centralized controller platform and its applications. Switches retain the forwarding work. A controller cluster can implement that single logical role across several machines, so the structural change is the control/forwarding boundary rather than a requirement for static ASIC rules or a ban on software routers.

See [SDN separation, logical centralization, and interfaces](../lessons/06_sdn/01_definition_and_interfaces.md).

questions.question: What is one advantage of SDN's programmable nature for large-scale data centers?
options: It requires proprietary hardware for each control rule
It prevents the use of encrypted protocols across tenants
It limits controller access to edge switches only
It enables dynamic traffic engineering via global policy updates
It ensures backward compatibility with all legacy protocols
questions.explanation:
A control program can use the network-wide view to express traffic-engineering policies and derive forwarding changes for multiple devices. That is more direct than separately adjusting every router's parameters and hoping distributed protocols produce the intended paths. It enables programmable policy changes, but does not automatically make multi-switch updates atomic or every legacy device compatible.

See [SDN separation, logical centralization, and interfaces](../lessons/06_sdn/01_definition_and_interfaces.md); [The Network OS and control programs](../lessons/06_sdn/08_network_os.md).

questions.question: Why is logically-centralized control considered beneficial in SDN?
options: It accelerates TCP three-way handshakes
It enables consistent global network views for decision-making
It prevents loops at the physical layer automatically
It reduces the number of packet headers per flow
It eliminates the need for any failover mechanism
questions.explanation:
The NOS presents a network-wide topology and state abstraction that control applications can use for coordinated decisions. That reduces how much distributed discovery and synchronization each application must implement itself. Consistency and freshness still depend on the platform: observations can be stale, controllers can fail, and switch updates need not happen atomically. A global view is an abstraction, not automatic loop freedom.

See [The Network OS and control programs](../lessons/06_sdn/08_network_os.md).

questions.question: How does OpenFlow determine how to forward packets in SDN?
options: By relying on VLAN IDs to infer routing intent
By hashing source and destination IPs to a random output port
By calculating shortest paths using Dijkstra’s algorithm at each switch
By assigning each packet a per-hop path label
By matching packet headers to flow table entries and executing actions
questions.explanation:
A switch compares supported packet-header fields with installed flow entries and applies the selected entry's actions, taking priority into account. The action may forward, drop, modify, or send traffic to the controller. This applies previously chosen forwarding state locally; it is not the same as running a shortest-path algorithm independently for each packet or picking random output ports.

See [OpenFlow matches, actions, counters, and capabilities](../lessons/06_sdn/12_match_action_tables.md).

questions.question: Which of the following statements best distinguishes out-of-band SDN control from in-band control?
options: In-band restricts control communication to TCP-based protocols only
In-band uses the same physical network for both control and data traffic
Out-of-band requires controller logic to be replicated at each switch
In-band routes control messages over a dedicated fiber-optic link
Out-of-band uses separate hardware for packet forwarding
questions.explanation:
In-band control carries controller/switch messages over the same forwarding links used by data traffic. Out-of-band control uses a separate management path, with physical isolation depending on how it is built. Sharing links can save infrastructure but introduces bootstrap and protection requirements; separate cabling adds cost. Neither arrangement requires a replica of the controller logic in every switch.

See [Out-of-band and in-band controller reachability](../lessons/06_sdn/16_control_paths.md).

questions.question: Which feature of the OpenFlow forwarding abstraction enables flexible packet handling?
options: The use of match-action entries over arbitrary packet header fields
An exact-match requirement for IP and MAC headers
Fixed-function hardware encoding of flow state
Periodic packet buffering before control decisions
A single static routing rule per destination prefix
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** Flexible match-action entries can inspect supported fields across several protocol layers using available exact matches and masks. The preserved key overstates this as arbitrary packet header fields: the OpenFlow version and switch capabilities limit what can be parsed and matched. The abstraction is more general than one fixed destination-prefix lookup, but it is not an unrestricted parser for every possible header.

See [OpenFlow matches, actions, counters, and capabilities](../lessons/06_sdn/12_match_action_tables.md).

questions.question: What is a primary benefit of introducing a Network OS and Hypervisor in SDN?
options: It reduces the control message size by replacing TCP with UDP
It enforces device-specific configurations
It abstracts distributed state into a unified global network view
It limits scalability to a single control program
It guarantees real-time forwarding even under high load
questions.explanation:
The NOS collects distributed switch, link, host, and counter information into a network-wide view; a hypervisor can additionally expose virtual views to tenants. Applications can work against these abstractions instead of each reimplementing distributed state management. This moves complexity into reusable platforms rather than eliminating it, and does not guarantee real-time forwarding or unlimited controller scalability.

See [The Network OS and control programs](../lessons/06_sdn/08_network_os.md); [Virtual topologies and physical policy enforcement](../lessons/06_sdn/10_virtual_topologies.md); [Moving complexity into reusable platform software](../lessons/06_sdn/11_reusable_complexity.md).

questions.question: In SDN-based access control, what is a key reason why routing changes can violate security policies?
options: SDN controllers cannot push updates to filters
Access control must be hardcoded into switch firmware
SDN lacks the ability to detect new links in the network
SDN does not support encryption between controllers and switches
Packet filters may not update automatically when topology changes
questions.explanation:
A route change can create a permitted forwarding path that bypasses a filter installed for the old path. In the lecture's narrow example, R3–R1–R2 can bypass the R5-filtered path from chi-FO toward nyc-DC. A correct SDN policy application must update enforcement coverage and ordering as topology changes; simply deploying SDN does not make ACL correctness automatic.

See [How a new route can bypass a packet filter](../lessons/06_sdn/06_routing_and_acls.md).

questions.question: Why is indirect control considered a challenge in traditional networking?
options: It requires changes to Ethernet frame format for routing decisions
It leads to complicated behavior when manipulating metrics instead of paths
It causes TCP flows to bypass firewalls unintentionally
It forces operators to manage encryption keys for each hop
It prevents use of static routes for performance tuning
questions.explanation:
With indirect control, an operator changes inputs such as OSPF link weights so the distributed routing algorithm will hopefully choose the intended path. Predicting the inverse relationship between those parameters and network-wide behavior can be difficult, especially when mechanisms interact. Directly expressing desired forwarding or policy avoids some of that indirection, although implementation and safe updates still require work.

See [Indirect control and uncoordinated updates](../lessons/06_sdn/04_traditional_control.md); [Data, control, and management responsibilities](../lessons/06_sdn/03_networking_planes.md).

questions.question: What role does the match-action paradigm play in OpenFlow's design?
options: It simplifies switching by enforcing static rule tables
It enables flexible packet handling based on header field values
It synchronizes flow entries across multiple controller instances
It limits forwarding to IPv4 and TCP headers only
It offloads control logic into network management software
questions.explanation:
Match-action rules associate supported header-field conditions with configurable packet-processing actions. Changing those rules changes handling without requiring a separate hardwired mechanism for every application policy. The primitive governs forwarding behavior; it is not itself a controller-replica synchronization protocol and is not restricted to just IPv4 and TCP.

See [OpenFlow matches, actions, counters, and capabilities](../lessons/06_sdn/12_match_action_tables.md).

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates the flexibility provided by OpenFlow rule actions?
options: A rule that uses TTL expiration to trigger routing updates
A rule that overwrites headers and multicasts to multiple output ports
A rule that schedules packet delivery based on server CPU load
A rule that copies flow state to external cloud storage in real time
A rule that encrypts all packets using built-in switch logic
questions.explanation:
The source explicitly combines rewriting header fields with sending a matching packet to ports 5 and 6. That demonstrates both packet modification and replication to several outputs. A drop-only rule or a single-port forwarding rule shows only a narrower action. Actual available modifications remain constrained by the protocol version and the switch's advertised capabilities.

See [OpenFlow matches, actions, counters, and capabilities](../lessons/06_sdn/12_match_action_tables.md).

questions.question: In the context of SDN, what does network virtualization enable for data center tenants?
options: Migration of virtual machines without any flow update requirements
Per-user QoS profiles stored at each access point
Real-time bandwidth guarantees enforced by hardware switches
Dedicated physical switches per tenant to ensure isolation
Tenant-defined topologies compiled into switch-level configurations
questions.explanation:
A network hypervisor lets a tenant describe a virtual topology and policies over shared physical infrastructure, then translates that description into device-level enforcement. A tenant may see one logical switch even when traffic crosses several physical switches. Isolation depends on correct mapping and coverage; virtualization does not imply a dedicated physical switch or require every physical switch to receive an identical rule.

See [Virtual topologies and physical policy enforcement](../lessons/06_sdn/10_virtual_topologies.md).

questions.question: Why does consistency among SDN controllers present a scalability challenge?
options: OpenFlow mandates controller replication for every data plane rule
Consistency requires frequent broadcast flooding of packets
SDN switches cannot handle large rule sets
Coordinating multiple controllers increases communication overhead
Controllers require global Ethernet frame synchronization
questions.explanation:
Controller replicas must exchange and coordinate state so their decisions and switch updates remain compatible. The NOS can hide much of that message passing behind a logical global view, but it still performs the underlying work. As the deployment grows, that coordination adds communication and processing overhead alongside event handling. Logical centralization therefore does not make consistency free or require flooding every data packet.

See [Scale, reliability, latency, consistency, and interoperability](../lessons/06_sdn/19_systems_challenges.md); [The Network OS and control programs](../lessons/06_sdn/08_network_os.md).

questions.question: What is a common interoperability challenge when introducing SDN into existing networks?
options: SDN requires IPv6-only transport for control traffic
All legacy switches must be upgraded to Layer 3 devices
Controller logic must be implemented in hardware firmware
SDN switches can only operate using MPLS labels
Traditional routers lack support for OpenFlow protocol
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** Integrating devices without a compatible exposed forwarding interface can prevent a controller from programming them like OpenFlow switches, while neighboring routing domains still need interoperability. The preserved key is too broad: traditional equipment is not universally incapable of OpenFlow, and SDN is not defined by mandatory OpenFlow use. The challenge concerns actual device/interface compatibility and domain integration, not an IPv6-only or MPLS-only rule.

See [Scale, reliability, latency, consistency, and interoperability](../lessons/06_sdn/19_systems_challenges.md); [From integrated appliances to an open network stack](../lessons/06_sdn/07_open_network_stack.md).

questions.question: Which development most directly contributed to SDN's separation of control and data planes?
options: The adoption of MPLS in core Internet routing
The creation of open interfaces between control and forwarding logic
The transition from IPv4 to IPv6 in enterprise networks
The shift to wireless mesh architectures
The rise of software firewalls on commodity hardware
questions.explanation:
An open interface to packet forwarding separates how control software specifies behavior from a vendor's integrated control implementation and hardware. That boundary is a core component of the horizontal SDN stack, along with a controller platform and usable network view. Migrating to IPv6 or adopting MPLS alone does not establish this control/data separation.

See [From integrated appliances to an open network stack](../lessons/06_sdn/07_open_network_stack.md).

questions.question: Why has SDN gained traction particularly in cloud and datacenter environments?
options: SDN mandates per-flow encryption by default, which benefits cloud services
OpenFlow provides native support for VMM hypervisors like VMware ESXi
The need for flexible, cost-efficient network management aligns with SDN's design
Datacenters demand rigid, hardware-defined routing structures
SDN allows real-time enforcement of multi-tenant CPU quotas
questions.explanation:
Large cloud operators need fine-grained control, manageable multi-tenant networks, and economical infrastructure. Merchant silicon, programmatic control, and practical use of existing switch tables align with those demands. The source presents their combination as drivers of adoption; it does not claim that SDN mandates encryption, controls tenant CPU quotas, or requires inflexible hardware-defined routes.

See [Merchant silicon, cloud demand, and virtualization](../lessons/06_sdn/18_adoption_drivers.md).

questions.question: Why is network virtualization considered the 'killer app' for SDN in large-scale deployments?
options: It enables stateless packet forwarding at the physical layer
It offloads controller computation to tenant VMs
It removes the need for any centralized control logic
It enables per-tenant custom topologies and policies on shared infrastructure
It allows consolidation of all tenant traffic into a single broadcast domain
questions.explanation:
Network virtualization lets many tenants define their own isolated topologies, address spaces, and policies over shared servers and switches. A hypervisor translates those views into physical configurations, creating a useful service operators are willing to deploy and buy. This is the source's commercial killer application, not the removal of centralized control or consolidation of every tenant into one broadcast domain.

See [Merchant silicon, cloud demand, and virtualization](../lessons/06_sdn/18_adoption_drivers.md); [Virtual topologies and physical policy enforcement](../lessons/06_sdn/10_virtual_topologies.md).

questions.question: What is the role of a network hypervisor in SDN-based virtualization?
options: It assigns MAC addresses based on OpenFlow rule priorities
It encrypts all traffic flowing through tenant routers
It maps virtual tenant topologies to concrete switch configurations
It schedules CPU cycles on shared switches among tenants
It dynamically tunes MTU values across tenant networks
questions.explanation:
The network hypervisor maps a tenant's abstract network and policy into configurations for the actual forwarding infrastructure. For example, one virtual A-to-B drop rule may require enforcement at selected physical ingress points that cover all relevant paths. It is a network-virtualization role, not CPU scheduling or a rule that MAC addresses follow OpenFlow priorities.

See [Virtual topologies and physical policy enforcement](../lessons/06_sdn/10_virtual_topologies.md).

questions.question: How does SDN manage network complexity through abstraction?
options: It pushes all routing decisions to the hardware switches
It converts IPv6 addressing into compressed IPv4 headers
It allows each router to execute its own independent control logic
It compiles routing rules into pre-shared MAC address sets
It shifts complexity from per-application logic into reusable SDN layers
questions.explanation:
The compiler analogy describes moving distributed state handling and topology translation into reusable NOS and hypervisor layers. Application-specific control programs can then express policy against a simpler graph or virtual topology. The underlying synchronization and mapping problems still exist, but many applications can share their implementation rather than each solving them independently.

See [Moving complexity into reusable platform software](../lessons/06_sdn/11_reusable_complexity.md); [The Network OS and control programs](../lessons/06_sdn/08_network_os.md); [Virtual topologies and physical policy enforcement](../lessons/06_sdn/10_virtual_topologies.md).

questions.question: In OpenFlow, what happens when a packet does not match any existing flow table entry?
options: The switch rewrites the packet headers to match known flows
The switch uses the default static route to handle the packet
The switch encrypts the packet and sends it to all ports
The packet is dropped immediately to preserve security
The switch forwards the packet to the controller for decision-making
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** In the lecture's example, a configured table-miss rule sends unmatched traffic to the controller using Packet-IN. That is an assumption, not an unconditional OpenFlow outcome. In OpenFlow 1.3, without a suitable table-miss entry the default is to drop unmatched packets. The preserved key therefore needs a version/configuration qualifier; a miss alone does not prove controller delivery.

See [Configured table misses, Packet-IN, and buffering](../lessons/06_sdn/13_table_misses.md).

questions.question: Which OpenFlow rule illustrates packet modification and multicast behavior?
options: Match on TCP port and drop the packet
Match on MAC address, send to controller
Match on VLAN tag and send to all ports except ingress
Match on header, rewrite fields, and forward to ports 5 and 6
Match on IP header, then forward to port 1
questions.explanation:
The rule that rewrites matching header fields and forwards to ports 5 and 6 includes both requested behaviors: modification and multiple-output delivery. Sending to the controller is a different action, and flooding without rewriting does not demonstrate modification. This describes the lecture's conceptual action combination, subject to the fields and actions a particular switch supports.

See [OpenFlow matches, actions, counters, and capabilities](../lessons/06_sdn/12_match_action_tables.md).

questions.question: How does OpenFlow support vendor-neutral SDN control?
options: It uses a standard interface to define forwarding behavior across devices
It requires controller logic to be compiled into each switch
It enables custom packet formats per vendor specification
It enforces use of a single hardware architecture
It mandates switches to expose proprietary APIs
questions.explanation:
A standardized forwarding interface lets control software describe supported behavior across compatible devices without depending on each vendor's private internal control API. The ISA analogy separates the program's abstraction from hardware implementation. Vendor neutrality does not require identical hardware or promise identical capabilities; the controller must still account for what each device supports.

See [A flexible, minimal, vendor-neutral forwarding abstraction](../lessons/06_sdn/09_forwarding_abstraction.md).

questions.question: What is the purpose of abstract network views in SDN virtualization?
options: To convert IPv6 traffic into IPv4 inside tunnels
To allow tenants to define logical topologies over shared physical networks
To enforce per-user firewall rules at physical switches
To ensure symmetric routing for all TCP connections
To obfuscate IP addresses for enhanced anonymity
questions.explanation:
An abstract view lets a tenant work with a desired logical topology even when its traffic is carried by a more complicated shared physical network. The hypervisor maps between those views and installs the needed enforcement. The purpose is topology and policy abstraction, not automatic IP-address anonymity, symmetric TCP routing, or mandatory translation between IPv4 and IPv6.

See [Virtual topologies and physical policy enforcement](../lessons/06_sdn/10_virtual_topologies.md).

questions.question: How are tenant-defined SDN policies implemented in the physical network?
options: The network hypervisor dynamically compiles policies into flow table entries
The switch firmware hardcodes access control lists at startup
Each tenant is allocated a separate physical switch via VLAN segmentation
SDN requires NAT-based routing between virtual and physical topologies
The controller spawns a VM for each switch rule
questions.explanation:
The hypervisor translates tenant policy and topology into physical enforcement rules. In the OpenFlow abstraction, those rules become match-action flow entries selecting traffic and specifying its treatment. Placement must cover relevant paths and tenant isolation; a virtual drop policy need not install the same entry on every switch. No separate physical switch or VM per rule is required.

See [Virtual topologies and physical policy enforcement](../lessons/06_sdn/10_virtual_topologies.md); [OpenFlow matches, actions, counters, and capabilities](../lessons/06_sdn/12_match_action_tables.md).

questions.question: Why is scalability a core challenge in SDN deployments?
options: Each switch must recompute shortest paths independently
All control logic must be compiled into ASICs per switch
Centralized controllers may become bottlenecks as network size increases
SDN requires a separate VLAN ID for each flow
Flow table entries are broadcast to all routers in the network
questions.explanation:
Switch events, topology changes, counters, and reactive flow requests create work for controller servers. More switches and flows can increase that load until decision elements become bottlenecks. Distributing the controller can help capacity and reliability but also introduces coordination concerns. The architectural separation of control and forwarding does not itself guarantee unlimited event-processing capacity.

See [Scale, reliability, latency, consistency, and interoperability](../lessons/06_sdn/19_systems_challenges.md).

questions.question: In an SDN network, what is a likely consequence of controller failure without a backup?
options: Packets continue to be forwarded based on stale flow rules
All switches broadcast packets to all ports to compensate
Controllers from other domains take over seamlessly
Switches automatically enter self-healing mode
Traffic is rerouted through the network management plane

questions.question: Which factor contributes to increased latency in SDN decision-making?
options: Synchronous updates of all flow entries every millisecond
Compiled routing logic embedded in end hosts
Per-packet controller intervention in initial flow setup
Lack of TTL decrement at data-plane switches
The use of copper instead of fiber cables
questions.explanation:
**Review note:** An initial reactive miss can require a remote Packet-IN/Flow-MOD exchange before forwarding proceeds, adding communication and decision delay. The preserved per-packet wording is misleading if applied to every packet in the flow: once matching rules are installed, later packets can be forwarded locally while those rules remain valid. The latency issue is the consultation path, not intrinsically the cable material.

See [Scale, reliability, latency, consistency, and interoperability](../lessons/06_sdn/19_systems_challenges.md); [Configured table misses, Packet-IN, and buffering](../lessons/06_sdn/13_table_misses.md); [Packet-OUT, Flow-MOD, and rule lifetimes](../lessons/06_sdn/14_controller_responses.md); [A reactive TCP and HTTP exchange](../lessons/06_sdn/15_reactive_handshake.md).

questions.question: What is the key challenge in maintaining consistency across multiple SDN controllers?
options: They use incompatible OpenFlow versions
SDN controllers must all share the same physical IP address
Controllers must synchronize updates to avoid conflicting flow rules
Flow tables cannot store more than 100 rules per switch
Each controller must act as an autonomous router
questions.explanation:
Multiple controllers can observe changes and issue updates at different times. Their state, ownership, and update decisions need coordination so they do not install incompatible forwarding behavior, particularly during failures or partitions. A single logical control plane does not make those replicas physically identical or eliminate synchronization. Compatibility between controller decisions is the challenge, not a universal 100-rule switch limit.

See [Scale, reliability, latency, consistency, and interoperability](../lessons/06_sdn/19_systems_challenges.md).
